> The new billing dashboard is live for everyone as of this morning. Find it under **Settings → Billing**.
>
> What you can do there now:
> - See usage and the running total for the current cycle, refreshed hourly
> - Download any invoice from the last [24 MONTHS] as PDF
> - Update the card on file yourself, no ticket
>
> The old invoice request form is retired. Anything you had open in it was migrated, so it should already be in your invoice list.
>
> If a number looks wrong, post in #billing-dashboard and tag me. Wrong numbers on a billing page are the kind of bug we want loudly, not politely.

**Notes**

- **The specifics are mine.** Refresh interval, invoice retention window, and the channel name are plausible fill-ins so it reads as a real message. Replace them before sending.
- **Add a screenshot.** A UI announcement without one gets three replies asking where the button is.
- **I assumed the migration is done and verified.** If the old form's open requests are still in flight, cut that paragraph rather than promise it.

> Code freeze runs the 20th through the 27th. Last merge to `main` lands 5pm on the 19th, your local time.
>
> During the window:
> - No merges to `main` except fixes for a Sev1 or Sev2
> - A hotfix needs a second reviewer and a note in #eng-freeze before it merges
> - Feature branches keep moving and PRs keep getting reviewed, they just wait to land
>
> Why: [REASON, e.g. holiday coverage is thin and on-call is one deep].
>
> If you think something has to ship inside the window, tell me by the 18th so we decide it now instead of at 11pm on the 23rd.

**Notes**

- **[REASON] is the one slot you have to fill.** A freeze with no stated reason reads as arbitrary and gets worked around.
- **I picked "Sev1 or Sev2" as the exception bar.** If your severity scale runs differently, or if the bar should be "customer-facing outage only", swap that line; it is the sentence people will argue about.
- **No deploy-freeze language included.** I wrote merge freeze only. If deploys are also frozen, that needs its own line, because the two are not the same thing to whoever is on call.

```
fix(payments): derive idempotency key per attempt group, not per retry

A timed-out charge that got retried could bill the customer twice. The
retry path generated a fresh idempotency key on every attempt, so the
gateway saw each retry as a new charge instead of a repeat of the
first one.

The key is now derived from the payment intent ID plus the attempt
group, so every retry of the same logical charge carries the same key
and the gateway collapses them.

- Move key generation into PaymentAttempt.idempotency_key
- Reuse the key across all retries within one attempt group
- Reject a new charge when the intent already has a succeeded charge

Fixes [ISSUE]
```

**Notes**

- **`PaymentAttempt.idempotency_key` is invented.** I do not have your code, so the symbol name and the third bullet are placeholders shaped like a real fix. Match them to what you actually changed.
- **The third bullet is a second layer.** If your hotfix is only the key change, delete it; a commit body claiming a guard that is not in the diff is worse than a thin message.
- **Worth saying in the body if true:** whether already-duplicated charges are refunded by this deploy or need a separate backfill. That is the first question anyone reading this commit in a month will have.

> **Deprecated: `GET /v1/[RESOURCE]`. Removal date: [DATE, six months out].**
>
> This endpoint is deprecated as of [TODAY'S DATE] and will be removed on [DATE]. After that date, requests to it return `410 Gone`.
>
> **What to use instead:** `GET /v2/[RESOURCE]`. It returns the same records with two differences: timestamps are RFC 3339 in UTC rather than epoch seconds, and results are cursor-paginated via the `next` field instead of `page` and `per_page`. Migration guide: [LINK].
>
> **What happens between now and then:** the v1 endpoint keeps working unchanged. Responses now include a `Deprecation` header and a `Sunset` header carrying the removal date, so you can catch remaining callers in your own logs.
>
> **Scheduled brownouts.** We will return `410` for a short window on two dates before removal, so a forgotten integration fails while someone is awake to see it:
> - [DATE], 15:00 to 15:15 UTC
> - [DATE], 15:00 to 16:00 UTC
>
> **If six months is not enough**, reply to this notice or contact [SUPPORT CHANNEL] before [DATE]. We would rather hear it now than on removal day.

**Notes**

- **Every bracketed slot and both v1/v2 differences are mine.** The timestamp and pagination changes are the kind of thing that usually differs between versions; replace them with the real diff or the notice will mislead people into a broken migration.
- **The brownouts are a recommendation, not a given.** They are the single most effective part of a deprecation and also the part that generates support load. If you skip them, cut the section rather than leave it vague.
- **One thing I would add if you have it:** a rough count of how many callers are still on v1. Publishing "fewer than 40 accounts still call this" turns an abstract deadline into someone's actual problem.

**Subject line, three takes:**

1. Plain: `Your [PRODUCT] account is ready`
2. Next-action: `Start here: your first project in [PRODUCT]`
3. Warm: `Welcome to [PRODUCT], here's the fastest way in`

I'd send #2. It sets an expectation the email then delivers on, and it beats #1 on open rate for the same honesty.

> Hi [FIRST NAME],
>
> Your [PRODUCT] account is ready. The fastest way to see whether it fits how your team works is to get one real project in there, not a test one.
>
> **Three steps, about ten minutes:**
>
> 1. **Create a project** and name it after something your team is actually working on this week.
> 2. **Add three or four tasks** with owners and due dates. Real ones, even if the list is incomplete.
> 3. **Invite one teammate.** [PRODUCT] gets useful at two people and dull at one.
>
> [Create your first project →]([LINK])
>
> A few things people miss in the first week:
>
> - **Import from [TOOL]** if you have a backlog somewhere else. It takes a couple of minutes and beats retyping. [LINK]
> - **Keyboard shortcuts:** press `?` anywhere to see them.
> - **Your trial runs until [DATE].** No card on file, and we'll email you before anything changes.
>
> If you get stuck, reply to this email. It reaches a person on the product team, not a queue.
>
> [SENDER NAME]
> [ROLE], [PRODUCT]

**Notes**

- **"Reply reaches a person" only ships if it's true.** It is the highest-trust line in the email and the easiest one to make a lie. If replies go to a shared inbox with a 48-hour SLA, say that instead.
- **Trial terms and the import source are invented.** Fill in [DATE] and [TOOL] from your actual plan setup, or drop those bullets.
- **I kept it to one call to action.** Welcome emails tend to accumulate links to docs, community, and the mobile app. Each one added lowers the odds of step 1 happening.

> Hi [NAME],
>
> I can't refund the [PLAN] charge from [DATE]. Our refund window is [30] days and that payment is [X] days past it, so it's outside what I'm able to reverse.
>
> Here's what I can do:
>
> - **Cancel the renewal now** so you're not billed again on [NEXT BILLING DATE]. You keep access through [END OF PERIOD].
> - **Apply a [AMOUNT] credit** to the account if you'd rather stay on and give it another cycle.
>
> Tell me which one and I'll take care of it today.
>
> One thing I'd like to know either way: [REASON YOU CANCEL / WHAT WENT WRONG] is worth more to us than the refund is worth to you. If something broke or didn't do what you expected, I'd rather hear it than not.
>
> [SENDER NAME]
> [ROLE], [COMPANY]

**Notes**

- **I wrote this as a firm no with two real alternatives.** A soft no ("unfortunately our policy...") invites a second email arguing the policy, which costs both of you another round.
- **The credit offer assumes you're allowed to make it.** If you aren't, delete that bullet; do not replace it with a vague "let me see what I can do", which is how a no becomes a maybe and then a complaint.
- **If the charge is under [30] days and someone miscounted, this whole reply is wrong.** Check the date before sending. Denying a refund that was actually in-window is the expensive version of this mistake.
- **The last paragraph is optional.** It reads as genuine when the answer is no and as deflection when the customer is already angry. Cut it if the thread has heat in it.

> ## Day one
>
> Goal for today: your machine builds the service and you have shipped one commit to `main`. Not a real feature, just proof the whole path works end to end. Most people finish by mid-afternoon; if you're still fighting the environment at 3pm, stop and ping your onboarding buddy rather than grinding.
>
> **Before you start:** you need your [COMPANY] Google account, laptop admin access, and your buddy's name. All three come from IT in your first-day email. If any are missing, that's step zero.
>
> ### Access (do these first, some take an hour to propagate)
>
> 1. **Sign in to Okta** and enroll in MFA. Everything else hangs off this.
> 2. **Request access** in [ACCESS TOOL] to: `github/[ORG]`, AWS `dev` account, [OBSERVABILITY TOOL], and PagerDuty (read-only for now, you're not on rotation for [4 WEEKS]).
> 3. **Join Slack channels:** #eng, #[TEAM], #deploys, #incidents.
>
> ### Environment
>
> 4. **Clone the monorepo:** `git clone git@github.com:[ORG]/[REPO].git`
> 5. **Run the bootstrap script:** `./scripts/bootstrap.sh`. It installs the toolchain, pulls dev secrets from [SECRETS TOOL], and seeds a local database. Expect [15 MINUTES].
> 6. **Run the tests:** `make test`. A clean checkout should be green. If it isn't, that's our bug, not yours; post the output in #[TEAM] and someone will pick it up.
> 7. **Start the service locally:** `make dev`, then confirm `curl localhost:[PORT]/health` returns `ok`.
>
> ### Your first commit
>
> 8. **Add yourself to `docs/team.md`**, open a PR, get it reviewed in #[TEAM], and merge it. This is deliberately trivial. What matters is that you have seen the review flow, CI, and the deploy pipeline once with nothing at stake.
> 9. **Watch it deploy.** Your merge triggers a deploy to staging. Follow it in #deploys so you know what a normal one looks like before you see an abnormal one.
>
> ### Reading, if you have time left
>
> - [ARCHITECTURE DOC] gives you the service map. Skim it, don't study it.
> - [ON-CALL RUNBOOK], same. You'll come back to it in week [4].
>
> **What we do not expect today:** understanding the domain, reading the whole codebase, or writing anything that matters.

**Notes**

- **Every tool name, path, and command is invented.** Bootstrap script, `make test`, `docs/team.md`, the tooling names. This is the shape of a good day-one checklist; you have to fill it with your actual stack or it will send someone down a path that doesn't exist.
- **Access first is deliberate.** Provisioning lag is the single most common reason day one turns into day three, and it's the one thing that can't be worked around by the new hire.
- **Step 8 is the load-bearing one.** If your pipeline can't safely take a trivial commit to `main` on someone's first day, that is worth knowing before you write it into a doc.
- **Left out on purpose:** the HR and benefits items. Those usually live in a separate checklist, and mixing them in makes the engineering half look optional.

> **File uploads failed for about 90 minutes on [DATE]. Uploads are working normally now. No files that were already stored were affected.**
>
> **What happened:** between [START TIME] and [END TIME] [TIMEZONE], attempts to upload files failed with an error or hung and timed out. Everything else in [PRODUCT] kept working, including access to files uploaded before the incident.
>
> **Cause:** [ROOT CAUSE, e.g. a configuration change to our storage service rejected requests larger than a certain size]. The change was rolled back at [TIME], and uploads recovered within [X] minutes.
>
> **What you should check:** any file you uploaded during the window may not have saved. Files that failed did not partially store, so there is nothing corrupted to clean up. If you got a success confirmation, the file is there. If you're unsure, the simplest check is to look at [WHERE, e.g. the project's Files tab] and re-upload anything missing.
>
> **What we're doing about it:** [SPECIFIC FIX, e.g. adding upload success rate to the alert that pages on-call, so this is caught in minutes rather than after customer reports]. We detected this from [DETECTION SOURCE], which is later than we want, and that is the part we're fixing first.
>
> Questions, or if you're still seeing upload failures, contact [SUPPORT CHANNEL].

**Notes**

- **Cause, detection source, and remediation are placeholders.** They are also the only three parts customers actually judge you on, so guessing at them in the published version is worse than posting a shorter note without them.
- **I asserted no data loss and no partial writes.** Verify both before sending. If failed uploads could have left partial objects, the "nothing corrupted" line has to go and the note needs a cleanup instruction instead.
- **I included that detection was slow.** Some teams cut that. It buys more credibility than it costs, but it's your call and it's the sentence a comms reviewer will flag.
- **No apology paragraph.** A clear timeline plus a specific fix reads as more serious than "we sincerely apologize". Add one line of apology at the top if that's your house style; don't add three.

> This is the annual engineering satisfaction survey. It takes about [10] minutes, it's anonymous, and it closes on [DATE].
>
> We use it to decide what to actually fix. Last year's results are why we [SPECIFIC CHANGE FROM LAST YEAR, e.g. cut the release process from four approvals to one and rebuilt the local dev setup]. That's the standard we're holding ourselves to again: results and what we're changing get shared with the whole org within [30] days of close, including the parts that aren't flattering.
>
> Answer honestly, especially where it's negative. A survey full of 4s tells us nothing and costs you ten minutes.

**Notes**

- **[SPECIFIC CHANGE FROM LAST YEAR] carries the whole paragraph.** If nothing visible changed after last year's survey, cut that sentence rather than fill it with something vague. People remember, and a vague claim lowers response rates more than no claim.
- **Anonymity has to be literally true.** If responses are tied to team and a team has three people, it isn't anonymous in practice. Either say "aggregated, and we don't report on teams smaller than [5]", or drop the word.

**Take one, plain:**

> Out Thursday and Friday, back Monday. [NAME] is covering [AREA] while I'm gone; anything urgent goes to them.
>
> I won't be checking Slack. If something's on fire and [NAME] needs me, they have my number.

**Take two, with handoff detail:**

> Out Thursday and Friday, back Monday.
>
> - **[PROJECT] review:** [NAME] has context and can approve.
> - **Anything on-call adjacent:** [NAME], I'm off the rotation those days.
> - **[PR/TICKET]:** waiting on [PERSON], not blocked on me.
>
> Not checking Slack. Genuinely urgent, [NAME] knows how to reach me.

I'd send take one unless you have real handoffs, in which case the list saves someone a search.

**Notes**

- **The [NAME] slot has to be someone who agreed to it.** Naming a cover in public before asking them is how you come back to a grudge.
- **"Not checking Slack" is worth keeping.** Vague PTO messages get you pinged anyway, which defeats the point.

> ## [VERSION], released [DATE]
>
> ### Added
>
> **Single sign-on (SAML 2.0).** Admins can now connect [PRODUCT] to an identity provider and require SSO for everyone in the workspace. Tested with Okta, Entra ID, and Google Workspace; other SAML 2.0 providers should work but aren't formally supported yet.
>
> - Set it up under **Settings → Security → Single sign-on**
> - Just-in-time provisioning is on by default; new users get created on first sign-in with the [MEMBER] role
> - SCIM directory sync is not in this release. It's on the roadmap for [QUARTER]
> - Available on [PLAN NAMES]
>
> Setup guide: [LINK]
>
> ### Removed
>
> **The legacy export button is gone.** It exported to [OLD FORMAT] and had been deprecated since [DATE].
>
> Use **Export** in the [LOCATION] menu instead. It covers everything the old button did plus [DIFFERENCE], and it handles workspaces over [SIZE] without timing out, which the old one didn't.
>
> **If you script against the old export**, the endpoint it called (`[OLD ENDPOINT]`) now returns `410 Gone`. Switch to `[NEW ENDPOINT]`. Migration notes: [LINK].
>
> ### Fixed
>
> - [FIX 1]
> - [FIX 2]

**Notes**

- **The removal needs more room than I gave it, if the old export had automated users.** Right now it's one paragraph in a release note. If people scripted against it, that's a breaking change and deserves its own email before the release, not a line in the changelog after.
- **Provider list, plan availability, and the SCIM timeline are mine.** Those three get quoted back at you by sales and support, so check each one.
- **I put Added before Removed.** If the removal is the thing more of your users will feel, flip them. Release notes are read top down and abandoned halfway.
- **Fixed section left as slots.** I don't know what else shipped.

**Subject:** `[VENDOR] integration blocked [X] weeks, need an owner`

> Hi [NAME],
>
> Our [PRODUCT] integration has been blocked for [X] weeks and I need your help getting it unstuck. The launch date we agreed to is [DATE], and at the current pace we're going to miss it.
>
> **Where it stands:** we're blocked on [SPECIFIC BLOCKER, e.g. sandbox credentials for the v2 API]. We opened ticket [TICKET NUMBER] on [DATE]. Since then:
>
> - [DATE]: first response, told it was being routed to [TEAM]
> - [DATE]: followed up, no reply
> - [DATE]: followed up again, told it was still in queue
> - [DATE]: no update since
>
> Our side is done and waiting. [WHAT'S BUILT] is complete and tested against [WHAT YOU COULD TEST AGAINST].
>
> **What I'm asking for:** a named owner on your side and a date by [DATE, 2-3 days out]. Not a resolution date necessarily, just someone who owns it and a realistic estimate. If the answer is that [BLOCKER] takes another six weeks, that's workable information; silence isn't.
>
> Happy to get on a call this week if that's faster. I'm free [TIMES].
>
> [SENDER NAME]
> [ROLE], [COMPANY]

**Notes**

- **The dated timeline is the part that works.** An account manager can forward four timestamps to an engineering lead and get action. "We've been waiting a while" gets forwarded nowhere. Fill those in accurately, including any gaps where your side was slow, because they'll be checked.
- **I asked for an owner and a date, not for the blocker to be fixed.** It's a smaller ask, harder to refuse, and it's the thing you're actually missing.
- **I left out contract leverage.** No mention of renewal, SLA, or escalating further. That's your call, and it's a one-way door in a relationship you presumably want to keep. If you want it in, one sentence at the end is enough, and it should be factual rather than pointed.
- **Check the launch date is still real before sending.** If your own team has slipped too, leading with a missed deadline invites the reply you don't want.
